q: A young widow took over her husband's Champagne house in 1805, ran it for more than half a century, and got a shipment through to Russia in 1814 ahead of every competitor. Who was she?
exp: She inherited a small merchant business in her twenties and turned it into an export house at a moment when war had closed most of Europe to trade. Champagne has produced a striking number of such figures, which is why the French word for widow appears on more than one label in the region.

q: Adding sugar to must before fermentation, so that a thin year finishes stronger, carries the name of the French chemist and government minister who publicised it around 1801. Who?
exp: Chaptal was Napoleon's minister of the interior and wrote a treatise on winemaking that put the practice in front of every grower in France. He did not invent it, and his real contribution was as much the spread of careful cellar method as the sugar he is remembered for.

q: Fermentation was taken to be a spontaneous chemical decay until a French chemist showed in the 1860s that living micro-organisms do the work. Who showed it?
exp: He had been asked to find out why so much French wine was spoiling, and found that particular organisms produced particular faults, which is the beginning of microbiology as much as of modern winemaking. Gentle heating to kill those organisms was worked out for wine long before it was applied to milk.

q: An equation published in 1810 set out the proportions in which sugar becomes alcohol and carbon dioxide, and every calculation of potential alcohol still rests on it. Whose equation?
exp: Roughly speaking a given weight of sugar yields about half its weight in alcohol, which is what lets a must weight be read off as a probable percentage before fermentation begins. Lavoisier had already shown that nothing is lost in the process; this put numbers to it.

q: A physician was commissioned by the French government in the 1860s to survey the vineyards of the entire country, and the cane-pruning system he recommended now carries his name worldwide. Who was he?
exp: His reports set down what every region grew and how it was pruned at a moment when nobody had written it all in one place. Training a vine to one or two canes off a low trunk was his prescription for a regular crop, and it became the default across France and far beyond it.

q: From the 1950s onward a Bordeaux oenologist pressed estates to pick on ripeness rather than the calendar, discard rotten fruit and control the malolactic, and the region's difficult vintages stopped being undrinkable. Who was he?
exp: He consulted for dozens of properties and taught two generations at the university in his city, and his insistence on sound fruit and clean cellars is now so ordinary that it is hard to see as an argument. It was one: growers had simply accepted that a wet year produced bad wine.

q: An edict of 1716 fixed the boundaries of four Tuscan wine zones and set up a body to police the use of their names in trade. Which ruler issued it?
exp: Chianti, Carmignano, Pomino and Val d'Arno di Sopra were the four, and the edict is usually cited as the earliest attempt anywhere to protect wine names by drawing a line on a map. Naming the ground and then controlling who may use the word is the whole idea appellation law was later built on.

q: Eighteenth-century governments in Tuscany, Hungary and Portugal all drew boundaries around wine regions within a few decades of one another, and for the same commercial reason. What was it?
opts: Duty on wine was being evaded at the ports
Growers had planted far more vines than the market could absorb
The church claimed a tithe on every harvest
Wine from elsewhere was sold under a famous name
exp: A name that sells is a name worth counterfeiting, and by the eighteenth century the famous ones were being stuck on anything that would pour. Every later system, from the French appellations to the European register, answers the same problem with the same two moves: draw the boundary, then control the word.

q: A Tuscan baron who had served briefly as prime minister of the newly united Italy set down a recipe for his region's red wine in 1872, and growers followed it for a century afterwards. Who was he?
exp: He experimented at his own estate for decades before publishing, and his prescription of one dominant black grape supported by another is the ancestor of the rules that govern the zone now. Cavour was pushing comparable work in Piedmont in the same decades, hiring a cellar master who turned Barolo from a sweetish wine into a dry one.

q: Champagne growers rioted in 1911, burning cellars in Ay and emptying vats into the street while troops were rushed in by rail. What had provoked them?
opts: Merchants were buying grapes from outside the region
An order required every vine to be grafted onto American stock
Growers were forbidden to sell to anyone but the cooperative
A new duty was imposed on every bottle shipped
exp: The vineyard had been cut back by disease while sales were rising, so wine from far outside the district was being blended in and sold under the region's name. A boundary had been drawn in law in 1908 and fought over from the day it appeared, the Aube demanding entry and the Marne resisting, and the riots bought only a compromise second zone; the question was not settled until 1927.

q: Growers around one southern Rhone village wrote their own production rules in 1923 and went to court to enforce them, and the lawyer and grower who led them is usually called the father of the French appellation system. Who was he?
exp: His charter did what no earlier boundary had managed: it settled not only where the wine could come from but which varieties were allowed, how ripe the fruit had to be and what would be thrown out. Courts upheld it, and a decade later the same architecture was applied to the whole country.

q: The first of the American afflictions reached Europe in the 1840s, greying the leaves and splitting the berries, and growers learned to beat it by dusting the vines with sulphur. Which disease was it?
exp: Powdery mildew is the English name for the same fungus, and it grows on the surface of the plant, which is exactly why a surface dusting defeats it. Sulphur remains the standard treatment and is permitted in organic viticulture, so the nineteenth-century answer is still the one in use.

q: Dying vines across the Midi in the 1860s baffled everyone until a botanist from Montpellier dug beside a failing plant rather than under it and found a yellow aphid on the roots. Who was he?
exp: Digging at the edge of the damage was the trick, since the insects abandon a vine once it is finished and leave nothing to find. He named the louse and then crossed to the United States to see how American vines lived with it, and what he learned there is the basis of the answer still used.

q: France decorated a Texan nurseryman in 1888 for the vine material he shipped across the Atlantic and for his advice on matching it to different soils. Who was he?
exp: The award was the Chevalier du Merite Agricole, and he earned it by knowing the wild American species better than anyone alive. That mattered because a vine that shrugs off the louse can still turn yellow and die in chalky ground, so matching the species to the soil, rather than merely finding something resistant, is what made the cure work in practice.

q: Production fell so far during the crisis that cellars were topped up with raisins, sugar and water, and in 1889 the French state answered with a statute. What did that law do?
opts: It banned the import of American vine material
It fixed a minimum price for a hectolitre
It defined wine as the product of fermented fresh grapes alone
exp: Watering, sugaring and fermenting imported raisins had all become normal, because the shortage had made them extremely profitable. Fixing what the word wine means is the necessary first move before any origin rule can mean anything, and France took it under the pressure of fraud rather than out of principle.

q: Vines along a Medoc roadside had been daubed with a conspicuous paste to stop passers-by helping themselves, and in 1882 a botanist noticed that those vines alone had escaped the new mildew. Who followed the observation up?
exp: The mixture had been made up out of whatever was in the farm shed, and it proved to be the first effective fungicide against downy mildew. It still carries the name of the region where it was noticed, and vineyards across Europe turned blue-green every summer for the century that followed.
